The Saturday Evening Post. Founded in Philadelphia in 1821, it is an American weekly magazine that became the most widely circulated periodical in the United States during the early twentieth century. It is the longest-continuously published magazine in American history, though it suspended from 1969 before being revived. Circulation peaked at over six million copies per week in the 1930s, making it the best-selling magazine of its era. The magazine employed Norman Rockwell as cover illustrator from 1916 to 1963, commissioning over three hundred paintings that became defining images of American identity. The Saturday Evening Post published serial fiction and short stories by major authors including F. Scott Fitzgerald, Sinclair Lewis, and Ring Lardner. The magazine became famous for its advertising pages. Advertisements were as eagerly awaited as editorial content and shaped modern consumer culture. The Post adopted the tagline America's Greatest Weekly and explicitly targeted the middle-class family market. The magazine was known for a conservative, patriotic editorial stance during World War II and the Cold War. Through Norman Rockwell's iconic covers and its advertising aesthetics, The Saturday Evening Post shaped mainstream tastes and values for middle-class America.
